units.source: In His discourse on the last things, uttered by Him on the Tuesday of the week of His Passion, Jesus solemnly forewarned His disciples that many would come in His name, saying "I am the Christ," who would deceive many; that there would arise false Christs and false prophets, who would show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect; that, therefore, if any man said to them, "Lo, here is the Christ," or "Lo, there," they were not to believe it (

Edersheim remarks: "Though in the multitude of impostors, who, in the troubled time between the rule of Pilate and the destruction of Jerusalem, promised Messianic deliverance to Israel, few names and claims of this kind have be en specially recorded, yet the hints in the New Testament, and the references, however guarded, in the Jewish historian, imply the appearance of many such seducers" (Jesus the Messiah, V, chapter vi; in 1906 edition, II, 446). The revolts in this period were generally connected with religious pretensions in the leaders (Josephus, BJ, II, xiii, 4--"deceived and deluded the people under pretense of Divine inspiration"), and, in the fevered state of Messianic expectation, can hardly have lacked, in some instances, a Mes sianic character. Edersheim remarque : « Bien que, parmi la multitude d'imposteurs qui, dans la période troublée entre le gouvernement de Pilate et la destruction de Jérusalem, promirent à Israël la délivrance messianique, peu de noms et de prétentions de ce genre aient été spécialement consignés, les indications du Nouveau Testament et les allusions, si réservées soient-elles, de l'historien juif impliquent l'apparition de nombreux séducteurs de cette sorte » (Jesus the Messiah, V, chapitre vi ; dans l'édition de 1906, II, 446). Les révoltes de cette période étaient généralement liées à des prétentions religieuses de leurs chefs (Josèphe, BJ, II, xiii, 4 — « trompaient et abusaient le peuple sous prétexte d'inspiration divine ») et, dans l'état fébrile de l'attente messianique, elles peuvent difficilement avoir été dépourvues, dans certains cas, d'un caractère messianique. units.source: The most celebrated case of a false Christ is that of Bar-Cochba (to give the name its usual form), the leader of the great insurrection under Hadrian in 132 AD (Eus., HE, IV, 6; for Jewish and other authorities, see the full account in Schurer, HJP, I, 2, pp. 297 ff, English Translation). The insurrection was on a scale which it required the whole force of the Roman empire to put down (compare Schurer). The leader's own name was Simon, but the title, "Bar-Cochba" ("son of a star"), was given him with reference to the pr ophecy in

units.source: Among the Jews themselves, in later times, many pseudo-Messiahs have arisen. An interesting account of some of these is given by Mr. Elkan Adler in his Introduction to the volume, Aspects of the Hebrew Genius (London, Routledge, 1910). "Such there had been," this writer says, "from time to time ever since the destruction of the Temple." In the 16th and 17th centuries, however, the belief in pseudo-Messiahs took new and remarkable shapes. Among the names mentioned is that of David Reubeni, or David of the tribe of Reuben (1524), who ultimately fell a sacrifice to the Inquisition. Under his influence a Portuguese royal secretary, Diego Pires, adopted the Jewish faith, changed his name to Solomon Molko, and finally proclaimed himself the Messiah. In 1529 he published some of his addresses under the title of The Book of Wonder. He was burned at the stake at Mantua. "Other Kabbalists, such as Isaac Luria and Chajim Vital and Abraham Shalom, proclaimed themselves to be Messiahs or forerunners of the Messiah, and their works and manuscripts are still piously studied by many oriental Jews." The chief of all these false Messiahs was Sabbatai Zevi, born at Smyrna in 1626. "His adventures," it is said, "created a tremendous stir in western Europe." He ultimately became an apostate to Islam; notwithstanding which fact he had a line of successors, in whom the sect of Donmeh, in Salonica, continue to believe. Another mentioned is Jacob Frank, of Podolia, who revealed himself in 1755 as the Holy Lord, in whom there dwelt the same Messiah-soul that had dwelt in David, Elijah, Jesus, Mohammed, Sabbatai Zevi, and his followers. Jewish literature in the 18th century is full of controversial writing connected with Sabbatianism. As a special source of information on modern false Messiahs among the Jews, Lange mentions the serial Dibhre 'emeth, or Words of Truth (Breslau, 1853-54).
units.target: Parmi les Juifs eux-mêmes, à des époques ultérieures, de nombreux pseudo-messies sont apparus. Un récit intéressant de certains d'entre eux est donné par M. Elkan Adler dans son introduction au volume Aspects of the Hebrew Genius (Londres, Routledge, 1910). « Il y en avait eu de tels », dit cet auteur, « de temps à autre depuis la destruction du Temple. » Aux XVIe et XVIIe siècles, cependant, la croyance aux pseudo-messies prit des formes nouvelles et remarquables. Parmi les noms mentionnés figure celui de David Reubeni, ou David de la tribu de Ruben (1524), qui finit par être victime de l'Inquisition. Sous son influence, un secrétaire royal portugais, Diego Pires, adopta la foi juive, changea son nom en Salomon Molko et se proclama finalement le Messie. En 1529, il publia certains de ses discours sous le titre The Book of Wonder. Il fut brûlé sur le bûcher à Mantoue. « D'autres kabbalistes, tels Isaac Luria, Chajim Vital et Abraham Shalom, se proclamèrent messies ou précurseurs du Messie, et leurs ouvrages et manuscrits sont encore pieusement étudiés par de nombreux Juifs orientaux. » Le principal de tous ces faux messies fut Sabbataï Tsevi, né à Smyrne en 1626. « Ses aventures », dit-on, « suscitèrent une immense agitation en Europe occidentale. » Il finit par apostasier en faveur de l'islam ; malgré cela, il eut une lignée de successeurs auxquels la secte des Dönme, à Salonique, continue de croire. Un autre personnage mentionné est Jacob Frank, de Podolie, qui se révéla en 1755 comme le Saint Seigneur, en qui habitait la même âme messianique qui avait habité en David, Élie, Jésus, Mahomet, Sabbataï Tsevi et ses disciples. La littérature juive du XVIIIe siècle abonde en écrits polémiques liés au sabbatéisme. Comme source particulière de renseignements sur les faux messies modernes parmi les Juifs, Lange mentionne la publication en série Dibhre 'emeth, ou Words of Truth (Breslau, 1853-54).
